mainEntity.name: How many calories should I eat to lose 1 pound per week?

acceptedAnswer.text: One pound of fat is roughly 3,500 calories. To lose 1 lb per week you need a 500 cal/day deficit — so if your TDEE is 2,500 calories, you'd eat 2,000 per day. For 0.5 lb/week, a 250 cal/day deficit. The calculator does this math automatically and projects your goal date.

A deficit of 10–20% below your TDEE is safe and sustainable for most people. Deficits above 25% can cause muscle loss, hormonal disruption, and metabolic adaptation that stalls progress. Never eat fewer than ~1,200 cal/day as a woman or ~1,500 cal/day as a man without medical supervision.

mainEntity.name: How accurate is the 3,500 calories per pound rule?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 3,500 cal/lb figure (7,700 cal/kg) is a useful approximation but not exact. As you lose weight your TDEE drops, so actual losses tend to slow over time and timelines stretch slightly. It's accurate enough for planning — expect small deviations and adjust every 2–4 weeks based on actual progress.

mainEntity.name: Does a calorie surplus mean I'll just get fat?

acceptedAnswer.text: A modest surplus (200–400 cal above TDEE) paired with consistent resistance training adds mostly muscle with minimal fat gain. Larger surpluses (>500 cal) produce faster scale gains but a bigger percentage ends up as fat. Beginner lifters can gain muscle on small surpluses; experienced lifters need patience — realistic max lean gain is 0.25 lb/week for men, less for women.

mainEntity.name: Should I change my calorie target as I lose weight?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. As your bodyweight drops, so does your TDEE. Recalculate every 10 lb lost (or ~6 weeks) and adjust your calorie target. The calculator bases its projection on a static TDEE — the actual timeline will be slightly longer, but re-running the math periodically keeps you on track.
